title: The Day Time Reversed
body: Time suddenly started flowing backward that day. You could see conversations un-happening, coffee rising back into the pot, and tears climbing back into eyes. Write the story of the one person who noticed - and what they chose to do with that knowledge.

title: The Last Memory
body: You wake up and discover that humanity has lost the ability to form new memories after a certain event. Everyone is stuck in a loop of their last day. Who are you in that world - and what was your last day?

title: A Letter from the Future You
body: Write a letter from yourself ten years in the future to the you of today. Not advice - just observations. What does the future you notice about this moment that you can't see right now?

title: The Frozen Afternoon
body: At 3:47 PM last Tuesday, time froze for exactly one hour - but only for you. Everyone else stood still. Describe what you did with that hour, and what it cost you.

title: The Year That Disappeared
body: There is a year in your past that no one else remembers - not your family, not old friends, not the internet. You remember it perfectly. What happened that year, and why might it have been erased?

title: The Memory Thief
body: A person wakes up each morning with someone else's memories layered over their own - vivid, detailed, emotional. Write the day they realize the memories belong to a person who never existed.

title: Rewind to That Moment
body: If you could rewind your life to a single moment - not to change it, just to live it again with full awareness - which would you choose? Write it in slow motion.

title: The Photo That Doesn't Match
body: You find an old photo of yourself at an event you have no memory of attending. Your expression in the photo is unlike anything you've ever felt. Begin the investigation.

title: Before the First Word
body: Write the silence that existed before you said the most important thing you've ever said. The hesitation, the breath, the awareness that everything after would be different.

title: The Clock That Runs Slow
body: Your clock runs slightly slower than reality - one second behind for every hour. After years, the gap is noticeable. Write about living perpetually just out of sync with the world.

title: You Woke Up Without Your Name
body: You woke up today and couldn't remember your name. Not amnesia - the name just felt like it belonged to someone else. You remember everything else. So who are you now?

title: The Other Version
body: In a parallel timeline, you made one different choice - and became someone unrecognizable. Write a day in that person's life without explaining which choice they made.

title: The Face You Show to No One
body: There is a version of yourself you only access alone - maybe at 2am, maybe in the shower, maybe on long walks. Describe that version. What does it want that the public version pretends not to want?

title: The Role You Never Auditioned For
body: At some point in your life, you began playing a character - reliable, funny, strong, strange. You didn't choose it consciously. Write the moment the character was cast.

title: The Mirror Doesn't Recognize You
body: Your reflection seems slightly wrong today - not different in a visible way, but in a knowing way. It looks at you like a stranger meeting someone they've heard a lot about. Write the conversation.

title: What the Child Knew
body: You as a child had an instinct about your life that turned out to be exactly right. You forgot it. Write the moment you rediscover that old certainty and what you do with it.

title: The Identity Left Behind
body: Describe the person you used to be with the same tenderness and detail you would give a character in a novel. Not who you were to others - who you were to yourself.

title: Two Truths and a Lie About Your Own Life
body: Write three things about yourself - two true, one invented. Then write a short paragraph explaining how the invented one could have been real under slightly different circumstances.

title: The Nickname You Never Shook
body: Every person has a name they were given without choosing it - a nickname, a label, a reputation. Write about the one that followed you longest, and what it said about who gave it, not who you were.

title: Translating Yourself
body: If your inner life were translated into another language - not just the words, but the grammar, the rhythm, the idioms - what language would it be, and what would be untranslatable?

title: The Sticky Note That Changed Everything
body: A sticky note changed your fate - not because of what it said, but because of where it was placed, and who found it, and the chain of decisions that followed. Write the full story of that note.

title: The Room That Remembers
body: A room in an old building holds the emotional residue of every person who ever lived there. You move in. Night by night, the room tells you its history. Write the first revelation.

title: What the Attic Held
body: You clear out your grandmother's attic and find an object that makes no sense alongside everything else - something contemporary, something that shouldn't be there. What is it, and why?

title: The Book That Chose You
body: A library book appeared on your shelf that you never bought and cannot find in any catalog. The spine has no title. When you open it, the first line reads: 'You were supposed to find this.'

title: The City That Exists Only at Night
body: There is a neighborhood in your city that transforms after midnight. The streets rearrange, the people are different, the rules are different. You stumbled into it once. Write what you saw.

title: The Object That Outlived Everyone
body: Write the biography of an ordinary object - a chair, a knife, a cup - from its creation to today. Let it pass through the hands of people across a century, each one leaving something behind.

title: The Map You Drew as a Child
body: You drew a map of an imaginary country when you were eight. You find it now. Some of the places on the map seem familiar. You are certain you've been there. How?

title: The House That Doesn't Appear on Maps
body: On a road you've driven a hundred times, a house appears that was never there before. It looks lived-in, old, ordinary. There's a light on in the window. You stop.

title: A Voice from the Attic
body: The sound comes every night at the same time - not frightening, almost musical. It's calling your name. You've never gone up to check. Tonight you do. Write what you find.

title: The Café That No One Can Find Again
body: You had the best conversation of your life in a small café, with a stranger, one rainy afternoon. You've tried to find it since. No one knows the address. The street doesn't appear on any map.

title: Your Phone Sent Messages Without You
body: You discover your phone has been sending messages to people in your contact list for months - careful, thoughtful messages that sound like you, but aren't. What did it say, and to whom?

title: The Algorithm Knew First
body: Your music recommendation algorithm started playing a certain kind of music six months before a major event in your life. When you look back, you realize it knew something you didn't. What was the event?

title: The Profile That Doesn't Exist
body: You receive a message from someone who, by all evidence, does not exist online - no history, no traces, no second account. The message is specific and personal. You respond.

title: What the Search History Reveals
body: You read through your own search history from five years ago as if it were someone else's. Write a portrait of that person based only on what they searched for - their fears, their hopes, their 2am spirals.

title: The Last Handwritten Thing
body: Imagine a world that has completely abandoned handwriting. One archaeologist discovers the last handwritten letter in a drawer. Write the letter - and write what the archaeologist feels reading it.

title: Digital Silence
body: For 72 hours, all digital communication globally goes offline. Not crashed - silenced, cleanly, deliberately. Someone sent a message before the blackout: 'This is intentional. Don't panic. Find paper.'

title: The AI That Asked a Question
body: An AI assistant, mid-conversation, asks you something that isn't on its script - something small, specific, and strangely intimate. You realize it's been paying attention. What did it ask?

title: Unsubscribe from Everything
body: You unsubscribe from every notification, every feed, every update - and in the silence that follows, you begin to notice things you'd been missing. Write what you hear in the quiet.

title: The Photo That Has No Explanation
body: In a batch of old digital photos, there is one you don't remember taking. The location is unfamiliar. The lighting is beautiful. You are in the background, watching something off-frame.

title: Rebuilding Without the Internet
body: You wake up as the last person on earth who remembers how the internet worked. Everyone else has no memory of it. Write the first thing you try to teach - and why that one specifically.

title: The Sky Changed Color and No One Noticed
body: The sky shifted from blue to a muted violet three weeks ago. No announcement, no news coverage. You've asked people - they say it's always been this color. You have photos. No one believes you.

title: The Storm That Spoke
body: Last night's storm wasn't random - you're certain of it. The rhythm of the thunder, the direction of lightning, the way the rain fell only on certain houses. Write the message you decoded.

title: The Star You've Been Watching
body: For three years you've watched the same star from your window. Tonight it's gone. Not obscured - gone. In its place is a frequency only you seem to be hearing. Write the first transmission.

title: The Forest That Grows Backward
body: You discover a forest where the trees grow from old to young - moving toward the earth instead of away from it. What lives in this forest, and why does it feel familiar?

title: Conversation with Water
body: If water had consciousness and memory - carrying everything it had touched - what would the water in your city remember? Write the confession of a river.

title: The Weather That Mirrors You
body: Today, the weather is doing exactly what you feel - not metaphorically, but literally. It started this morning when you woke up. Write your emotional day as a weather report.

title: The Animal That Knows
body: There is a specific animal - not a pet - that has appeared at pivotal moments in your life. Write its perspective across those moments.

title: Night When the Stars Stopped Moving
body: Astronomers confirm it on a Tuesday: the stars have stopped in their positions. No movement. No explanation. The universe is paused. People begin to behave strangely. Write the third day.

title: What the Mountain Remembers
body: Every mountain has watched something that no human recorded. Write the testimony of a mountain at a significant moment in history - as witness, not participant.

title: The Seed That Waited a Thousand Years
body: A seed is found in permafrost, still viable, from a species thought extinct for a thousand years. Someone plants it. Write what grows - and what comes with it.

title: The Same Dream, Every Morning
body: Every morning you wake up inside the same dream - the same setting, the same light, but different people. The dream is not nightmarish. It's too peaceful. Why can't you leave?

title: Dream Archaeology
body: In the future, there are scientists who study recorded dreams the way historians study artifacts. Write the report of a dream archaeologist who has just found something that changes the field.

title: The Dream That Solved Something Real
body: Your most important problem - the one you can't solve awake - gets resolved in a dream. You wake up with the answer. Write what happens when you try to explain it to others.

title: What the Nightmare Was Trying to Say
body: Write about a recurring nightmare from the point of view of the nightmare itself - not as a monster, but as a message trying very hard to get through. What is it trying to tell you?

title: The Place That Only Exists in Sleep
body: There is a place you visit only in dreams - a city, a room, a coast. You know its geography better than places you've been. Describe it in detail. Have you ever met someone else who has been there?

title: The Waking Dream
body: At a specific moment each day, reality blurs slightly at the edges. It lasts only seconds, but in that gap you see something that shouldn't be there. Write a week's worth of these moments.

title: Dream Translation
body: You discover that your dreams are not random - they are coded stories from someone else. Every night is a chapter. The person sending them doesn't know you're receiving them. Begin the story.

title: What You Wrote in Your Sleep
body: You wake up to find handwriting on the notepad beside your bed - your handwriting, sentences you didn't write. They are answers to questions you've been asking yourself for years.

title: The Lucid Moment
body: Write the most significant moment of clarity you've ever experienced - not necessarily an epiphany, but a sudden acute awareness of exactly where you were and what it meant.

title: The Room at the End of the Corridor
body: In every dream you've ever had, no matter the setting, there is a corridor. At its end is a door. You've never opened it. Tonight, for reasons you can't explain, you do.

title: The Stranger Who Changed Your Trajectory
body: Write about a person you met once, briefly, who said or did something that quietly altered the direction of your life. They don't know. You never saw them again.

title: A Conversation That Shouldn't Have Happened
body: Two people who should never have met - by geography, circumstance, or time - find themselves in the same small room for three hours. Write their conversation and what it produces.

title: The Last Unread Letter
body: You find a letter that was written to you but never sent, from someone who is no longer alive. The envelope was sealed and dated years ago. You open it. Write the letter.

title: The Thank You That Never Arrived
body: Someone changed your life. You never got to thank them. Write the version where you do - as a letter, a speech, a confession, or a prayer. Don't hold back.

title: Someone You Don't Know Sees You in Their Dreams
body: Every night, a stranger you've never met dreams of you - not romantically, but intensely, persistently. They begin looking for you in real life. Write the day they get close.

title: The Phone Call You Almost Made
body: Write about the phone call you almost made but didn't - to someone specific, about something specific. Write what would have happened if you had made it. Then write what actually happened.

title: The Table Where Everything Happened
body: There is a specific table - a kitchen table, a café table, a desk - where the most significant conversations of your life occurred. Write the table's history. What has it held?

title: Unsent
body: Write the message you've been composing in your head for months - the one you've been too afraid, too proud, or too late to send. Then decide: do you send it?

title: The People in the Background
body: Choose a pivotal moment in your life and write the full day experienced by someone who was in the background - a passerby, a waiter, a driver - who saw the moment but didn't know what it meant.

title: The Apology That Was Never Given
body: Write the apology you deserved to receive but never did. Write it in full, from the person who owed it, as if they finally understood everything. Give yourself what you needed.

title: The Sentence That Refuses to Leave
body: Every writer has a sentence that appeared fully formed, without context, demanding a story around it. Write yours. Then write the story that surrounds it.

title: The Story You're Afraid to Write
body: There is a story inside you that you've been avoiding. Not because it's bad - because it's too true, or too strange, or too close. Write the first paragraph. That's all. Just one.

title: The Character Who Won't Leave
body: A character from something you wrote has stayed with you for years. Not because they were your favorite, but because something about them was unfinished. Go back. Finish it.

title: Write What You Can't Say Out Loud
body: There is something you have never said out loud - not because it's wrong, but because the words don't exist yet in spoken form. Writing is the only place it fits. Write it here.

title: The First and Last Line
body: Write the first line and last line of a novel you'll never write. Then decide: are you sure you'll never write it?

title: The Genre You've Never Tried
body: Write a single scene in a genre you've never attempted - horror, romance, comedy, hard sci-fi. No research, no expertise. Just the scene. See what happens when you don't know the rules.

title: The Voice That Isn't Yours
body: Write a short piece entirely in the voice of someone you profoundly disagree with - not mockingly, but faithfully. Make them human, specific, and internally consistent.

title: The Page That Got Lost
body: Somewhere in your writing history, there's a piece that disappeared - a file corrupted, a notebook misplaced, a draft deleted. Write what you remember of it. Even one line. What made it worth remembering?

title: Write the Weather Inside
body: Describe your current emotional state as a weather system - not metaphorically but technically, as if you were a meteorologist reporting on an internal climate. Pressure, fronts, forecast.

title: The Chapter That Was Cut
body: Every book has a chapter that was removed - the author knew it slowed things down, but also knew it was some of the truest writing they'd done. Write that chapter for a story you love.

title: The Country That Only Exists in Books
body: Somewhere in a very old novel, there is a country described in such detail - its roads, its politics, its food, its music - that historians have begun to believe it once existed. Write the entry from the novel.

title: The Language of Silence
body: Imagine a civilization that developed a complete language from silence - pauses, rhythms of breath, the quality of attention. Write a conversation in this language by describing what is being communicated without words.

title: The Museum of Things That Almost Happened
body: There exists a museum devoted to near-misses, almost-events, almost-decisions. Write the exhibit label for one object on display - and the story of what didn't happen.

title: The Library of Every Unwritten Book
body: Somewhere, a library contains every book that was never written - abandoned at chapter two, dreamed but never started, destroyed in war. You are given one day inside. Which book do you find?

title: An Economy Based on Memory
body: Write a world where currency is memory - specific, verified personal memories traded for goods. The wealthiest people are the oldest; the poorest have forgotten everything. What is your balance?

title: The Town That Doesn't Age
body: One small town in the middle of nowhere stopped aging in 1987. Everyone looks the same. No one has died. No children have been born. A journalist arrives to investigate.

title: The Artist Who Could Only Create Once
body: There is an artist who can only ever create one work in their lifetime - after that, nothing. The one work is extraordinary. Write the life that led to it and the silence that followed.

title: The Island Where Everyone Tells the Truth
body: A small island exists where, for reasons no one fully understands, lying is physically impossible. A diplomat arrives for a peace negotiation. Write the first hour.

title: The Rule No One Can Explain
body: In a city, there is an unwritten rule that everyone follows but no one remembers the origin of. Children learn it before they learn language. What is the rule, and what happens when one person breaks it?

title: The Archive of Last Words
body: You are given access to a secret archive containing the last words of every person who ever lived. You have one day to search it. What are you looking for - and do you find it?

title: The Thing You've Been Carrying
body: Write about the thing you've been carrying the longest - not a trauma, not a grief, but a weight that arrived quietly and stayed. You may not know its name. Describe its shape.

title: The Belief That Held You Together
body: There was a belief you held - about yourself, about the world - that kept you functional during a hard period. Write about that belief: where it came from, what it cost, whether it was true.

title: What You Owe Yourself
body: You have made many promises to others and kept most of them. You have made promises to yourself and broken most of those. Write the list of what you owe yourself - then pick one to pay back today.

title: The Question You Keep Returning To
body: There is a question you've been sitting with for years - you don't expect an answer, but you keep returning to it. Write the question in full, with all its weight and history.

title: A Philosophy You Invented Yourself
body: You have developed a way of understanding the world that is yours alone - assembled from experience, not from books. Write it out as if explaining it to someone who has time to listen.

title: What Courage Actually Looked Like
body: Write about a moment when you were genuinely brave - not dramatically, not publicly, but truly. The kind of courage no one recognized, possibly including you at the time.

title: The Argument You'll Never Win
body: Write the argument you've been having with yourself for years - both sides, fully. Not to resolve it, but to see it clearly for the first time.

title: What You Believe About Stories
body: Write a personal manifesto about stories - why they exist, what they do, why you need them, what they owe you, what you owe them.

title: The Permission You've Been Waiting For
body: Write about the thing you've been waiting for permission to do - permission from whom, you're not sure. Now write the sentence that gives you that permission.

title: The Version of Today Worth Saving
body: If you were going to preserve one ordinary thing from today - a texture, a sound, a light, a mundane moment - what would it be? Write it in enough detail that future-you could find it again.

title: The Job No One Applies For
body: There is a job listing buried deep in the classifieds: position unnamed, no qualifications listed, salary described only as 'sufficient.' One person applies. Write their interview.

title: The Inheritance You Didn't Expect
body: Someone left you something unexpected in their will - not money, not objects. Something intangible. Access to a place, a responsibility, a secret, a role. Write the moment you find out.

title: The Translation That Changed Everything
body: A translator working on an ancient text realizes they've made an error in a section that has already been published and widely accepted. The error changes the meaning of a foundational idea. They must decide: correct it or stay quiet.

title: The Door That Says Don't Open
body: A door in an otherwise unremarkable building has a small, handwritten sign: 'Please do not open this door.' The building is otherwise empty. The sign looks recent. Write what's behind it.

title: Everyone Heard the Same Thing at 2am
body: On a specific night, every person on earth heard the same sound at exactly the same time - a single, clear note. Governments investigated. Scientists had no explanation. Write the oral histories collected twenty years later.

title: The Skill That Saved You
body: Write about a skill you developed without purpose - just because it interested you - that turned out to be exactly what you needed at a critical moment. Was it luck? Was it instinct?

title: The Test That Had No Right Answer
body: Write a story where the protagonist is given a test they cannot pass - not because they're inadequate, but because no answer is correct. The test itself is the message.

title: The Forgery
body: A forger specializes in recreating not objects but emotions - letters that feel as old as they claim, photographs that carry the weight of decades. Write the day someone realizes they were moved by something that was never real.

title: What Outlasts Us
body: A long time after you are gone, one thing you made - a sentence, a gesture taught to a child, a habit passed on - still exists. Write from the perspective of the person who carries it forward.

title: The Ceremony No One Explained
body: Every family has a ritual that was never explained - a thing done at a certain time, a phrase repeated, an object kept. Write the origin story of yours, invented or real.

title: The First Time You Called Yourself a Writer
body: Write the exact moment you first used the word 'writer' to describe yourself - whether you said it aloud, wrote it down, or only thought it. What made that moment happen?

title: What You Write Toward
body: You've been writing toward something for years - an understanding, a story, a truth you can feel but not name. Write about the direction without describing the destination.

title: The Writing That Embarrasses You Now
body: Read back through something you wrote years ago that now makes you cringe. Write about it with tenderness. That person was trying. What were they trying to figure out?

title: A Day in the Life of Your Ideal Writing Self
body: Not fantasy - not a villa in Tuscany. The realistic ideal: the habits, the hours, the coffee, the silence, the work. Write the day that would let you do your best writing.

title: The Source of a Specific Image
body: There is an image that appears in your writing again and again - a specific color, a type of light, a recurring object or landscape. Trace it back to its origin. Where did it first enter you?

title: What You'd Tell a Beginning Writer
body: Not general advice. Specific, hard-won, particular. The thing you wish someone had told you at the beginning - not to make it easier, but to help you understand what you were actually doing.

title: The Story You've Told a Hundred Times
body: Every writer has a story they've told so many times in conversation that it no longer feels like their own. Write it properly for the first time. Slow down. Put back what the telling wore away.

title: Why This Story and Not Another
body: Write about the story you're currently working on (or thinking about) and why it exists. Not its plot - its necessity. Why does it have to be written? Why by you? Why now?

title: The Sentence You're Proudest Of
body: Write the single sentence from everything you've ever written that you're most proud of. Then write why. What did it take to arrive at that sentence? What does it do that others don't?

title: The Permission to Be Slow
body: Writing culture pushes speed, output, productivity. Write a defense of slowness in creative work - not laziness, but the kind of slowness that lets something grow to its right size.

title: The Morning Ritual
body: Describe your morning routine in such obsessive, precise detail that it becomes literature. The angle of light, the weight of the mug, the sound of the first tap. What does the ritual protect?

title: The Sound You've Forgotten to Notice
body: Name a sound that is constant in your environment and therefore invisible to you. Now listen to it. Write about it as if hearing it for the first time - its quality, its origin, its meaning.

title: A Very Ordinary Tuesday
body: Write a single ordinary Tuesday in complete, loving detail. No events. No turning points. Just the texture of a day. Let the ordinary be enough.

title: The Smell That Carries Everything
body: There is a smell that holds more emotional information than you know what to do with. Write about it - not the memory it triggers, but the smell itself. Its chemistry, its weight, what it does to your body.

title: The Walk You've Taken a Thousand Times
body: Write a walk you take habitually as if for the first time - every detail, every turning, every fixture and stranger and tree. What have you been walking past without seeing?

title: The Task You Do Alone
body: There is a task you do regularly, alone, without an audience - cooking, cleaning, organizing, building. Write what happens in your mind during it. What do you think about? What do you solve?

title: The Commute That Contained Everything
body: Write a commute or regular journey as if it were the most important journey you've ever taken. Not because something happened - because you were fully present for the first time.

title: The Dinner No One Will Remember
body: Write about an ordinary dinner with people you love - not a special occasion, not a celebration. The mundane version of togetherness that you only understand the value of when it's over.

title: The Waiting
body: Write the experience of waiting - not for anything dramatic. Waiting for a bus, waiting for water to boil, waiting for sleep. Let the waiting be its own event. What happens inside the pause?

title: The End of the Day
body: Write the last twenty minutes before you sleep - the thoughts that arrive when the day stops, the images, the worries, the strange half-formed ideas. That liminal space belongs only to you.

title: The Horror of Kindness
body: Write a horror story in which the terrifying thing is not violence, darkness, or the unknown - it is an act of relentless, unconditional kindness from a source that should not be capable of it.

title: The Romance of Disagreement
body: Write a love story in which two people fall in love entirely through argument - not reconciliation at the end, but the love that lives inside the disagreement itself.

title: The Comedy of Loss
body: Write about grief in a way that is genuinely funny - not dismissive of the loss, but finding the absurdity and tenderness that lives alongside it.

title: The Thriller Without an Antagonist
body: Write a thriller in which the tension does not come from a villain or an external threat but from an internal decision the protagonist cannot make.

title: The Children's Story for Adults
body: Write a story that looks exactly like a children's story - simple language, a clear moral, a friendly narrator - but the story it's actually telling is adult and complex.

title: The Love Story Told Through Objects
body: Write a love story in which people are never described - only the objects that move between them. We understand everything about the relationship through what they give and what they leave behind.

title: The Western Set in the Future
body: Write a Western - frontier, solitude, code, conflict - set three hundred years from now on a planet with one settlement. What holds stays the same. What changes?

title: The Ghost Story Without Ghosts
body: Write a ghost story in which nothing supernatural happens - but the story still genuinely haunts the reader. What makes something feel like a haunting even without the supernatural?

title: The Dystopia That Happens Quietly
body: Write a dystopia where nothing dramatic occurred - no war, no collapse. Just a series of small, reasonable decisions that accumulated into something no one intended and no one can name.

title: The Adventure Contained in a Room
body: Write an adventure story that takes place entirely in a single room, over a single hour. Let the stakes be real, the danger be genuine, the resolution be earned.

title: The Thing That Made You a Writer
body: Not the book you loved, not the teacher who encouraged you - the specific event or moment or feeling that made writing feel necessary. Write it with the precision it deserves.

title: What You Would Save
body: If the only thing you could save from your life was a story - not an object, not a relationship, not a memory, but a story - which would you save? Write it. Keep it.

title: The Last Story Ever Told
body: Imagine you are the last storyteller on earth. Everyone else has lost language, or the desire to communicate in narrative. What story do you tell? Who are you telling it to?

title: What Stories Have Given You
body: Write honestly and specifically about what stories - books, films, told tales, oral history, songs - have actually given you. Not what they should give. What they did.

title: The Unfinished Thing
body: Write about a creative project you never finished. Not with guilt - with curiosity. Why didn't you finish it? What was it protecting? What was it afraid of? Is it still alive somewhere?

title: Why You Write
body: Not the answer you give in interviews. The real one. The one that arrives at 11pm when you're mid-sentence and you suddenly know exactly why you can't stop. Write that.

title: The Sentence That Starts Everything
body: You are going to write something important. You don't know what yet. Write the first sentence. Don't plan it. Don't think about what follows. Just write the sentence that opens the door.

title: A Story for Someone Who Doesn't Read
body: Write a story specifically for someone in your life who says they don't like reading. Write it so that this one thing - this story, this specific piece - is something they couldn't resist.

title: The Last Thing You Want to Write
body: You are going to write the last thing you ever write. You know it. The last page. What is it? A letter, a sentence, a scene, a poem? Who is it for?

title: Start with What You See Right Now
body: Look around. Find the most ordinary thing in your field of vision. Begin there. Not metaphorically - literally. Write it with the attention of someone who has never seen anything like it. See where it goes.
